diagnosis.balance: River & far bank is 7 back (#23) and the most starved; Plaza & quay 6 back (#24); Cross street & allotments 5 back (#25). Courtyard 3 back, Sky 2, Lane 1, People 0. The starvation has concentrated on the east half of the map: River and Plaza together have had 2 of the last 7 iterations and hold 11 of the 49 inventory entries, against 21 for Sky and People. This batch puts b31 in River, b32 in Plaza and b33 in Street — the three starved domains, in order — and gives Sky only b30, which is observer work rather than more weather. b34 lands in People x Interaction/UX, a cell that has never been touched at all.

rationale:
Rung 2 — deepen and interconnect. There is no stall signal, all five of the last batch shipped, and the ladder says stay low when work is landing; the rung-5 climb at pass #25 did its job and does not need repeating.

What that climb left behind is the first brief. #26 named the season in the sill, #27 named whatever is under the pointer, #28 turned the season into a button that reaches midwinter in 19.6 real seconds. Those three are the answer to the thirty-second-viewer question and the loop built them well. Every one of them is SILENT. There is exactly one invitation in this town and it is about clicking the canvas; the button is advertised by a chevron and a cursor, and on a phone it is 10px uppercase in a caption slot. LAWS.md has carried "a feature that exists may exist at a rate of zero — advertise it or nobody finds it" since #13, marked as paid for three times, and the loop shipped a fourth instance of it the iteration after reading it. A law re-violated by the iteration that read it is stated but not REACHABLE at the moment of the decision, and the honest response is not to write it a fourth time — it is to spend a brief closing the instance and put the pattern in WATCH, where a brief-writer meets it. b30 does the first; this pass did the second.

b31 is the bet. The far bank has had a BANDSTAND since before the loop began and nothing has ever happened in it — a structure with no event, in the domain that is 7 iterations back, on a map whose whole east side has no gathering of any kind. Every crowd this town has is transient: walkers passing, browsers circling a stall, sitters who claim one seat each. An audience is a different shape — people who arrive for a thing, stand still together, and leave when it ends — and the loop has never built one. It is genuinely risky: it needs its own arrival source rather than a wider band (the rate-of-zero law), it needs the 0.9-cell separation to hold for a STANDING group where cue c49 says the guarantee is only at spawn, it needs staging as clamps on one progress so it packs away, and it should be summer-weighted so the green is empty in February. It may fail. It is the only one in this queue that could, and a queue of five safe jobs is how a loop grinds to a halt in comfort.

b32 spends the other half of the same observation. Nine systems read season() and every single one is west of the bridge or in the sky: the courtyard beds, the trees, the working day, the population caps, the weather, the river. The plaza, the fountain and the quay are identical in February and August — exactly the position the market was in before #29, which was the best-received connect in the run. The fountain is the plaza's landmark and the obvious seasonal reader.

b33 is small, and it is a correctness fix that a shipped feature turned into a visible falsehood. The opening scatter puts ornamentals into the allotment block (seed 42 opens with a fern in the plots) because speciesFor() filters only NEW sowing; since #29 the harvest walks that produce to a market board, so the town can now put a fern on a vegetable stall. It goes fourth rather than first because it is cheap and the three ahead of it are worth more to a viewer.

b34 finishes #27. The naming names ground, plants and trees; the walkers, ducks, swans, the sweeper and the boat all pass under the same pointer and answer with the paving they are standing on. __entities() already carries every one of them with a stable id, and crowns[] is the established pattern for letting the draw pass record where it painted a thing. It lands in People × Interaction/UX, a grid cell that has never been touched.

Curation was the larger half of this pass, and the finding is worth recording because it is the third time I have written a version of it. The budget was 51.0 KB against a 46 KB cap and is 44.1 now. But the number that matters is that it was 45.3 KB at the end of pass #25 and re-grew at 1.3 KB per iteration. I had capped and ENFORCED the two files I was watching — LAWS.md at 12 KB, ledger entries at 3 KB — and the growth went to the one file with no cap at all. state.json's inventory had reached 11.4 KB, larger than LAWS.md, because every landed iteration adds a system to it by construction and nothing ever said what a system costs. That is the Solvista failure's exact shape, which the budget script was written to prevent: cap one file and the growth relocates. So the fix is not more distilling. Inventory entries are now capped at 300 B each and measured by rotate-ledger.mjs, which names offenders the way it already names fat ledger entries; open cues are capped at 8; a single law is capped at 900 B, because a law that sprawls past a paragraph is two laws pretending to be one and reaches the file cap without anybody deciding to spend it. Inventory came down 11.4 → 8.5 KB by dropping measurements, which its own header had said belonged in the ledger since the day it was written.

LAWS.md: 12.0 → 11.5 KB, 26 → 25 laws, four promotions from #27–#30 absorbed. #29 and #30 both went in as MERGES into the probe-rewind law, and #29 is the better kind of promotion — it says the existing rule was right for the wrong reason (it is not that the sim keeps running, it is that the RENDERER draws from the PRNG), so the law is now correct rather than merely useful. #27 and #28 merged into one new law, "the sill is DOM, and DOM fails quietly", which closes a real gap: three of the last four iterations touched the sill and the loop had no law about it. #30 is the second new law, "a zero is evidence only if you show the test can be non-zero" — about proving a negative, and it generalises well past the seats work. To pay for them I split the slow-scalar law (1255 B, carrying two ideas — duration-is-not-rarity is now its own law), merged locate-before-you-judge into compare-against-a-control, folded "end a population by not deleting what is on screen" out of the split-flag law into time-compression where inflow-versus-standing-population already lives, and cut "a screenshot cannot see motion" into the filmstrip law. The weakest thing cut outright was the rest of the split-flag law — its "fade the largest thing first" clause, which was a filmstrip observation duplicating the filmstrip law.

One note for the record. #29 derived hysteresis independently for the third time, through a market store rather than a scalar or a moving object, and found something the first two did not: two lags COMPOSE, and the composition moved the year's trough from winter to spring, which nobody wrote. That is the loop generalising a law rather than re-deriving it, and it is the clearest evidence in this run that the memory is doing its job. The law now names a store as a third carrier.

queue.brief: There has been a BANDSTAND on the far bank since before the loop began and nothing has ever happened in it. The whole east side of the map has no gathering of any kind — every crowd this town has is transient, people passing through or claiming one seat each. Put something on in the bandstand on a summer afternoon and let people come and stand for it: an audience that arrives, holds still together, and thins when it ends. The green should be busy in July and empty in February.
queue.successLooksLike: Across a folded multi-year probe, a summer afternoon puts a legible standing group at the bandstand and midwinter puts none; the audience arrives over minutes rather than appearing, reads as separate people rather than one shape at every moment it is on screen, and packs away when the thing ends without anybody teleporting. A filmstrip of the far bank shows no POP at set-up or strike.
queue.avoid: Do not widen an existing spawn band to feed it — the east half already shares one budget, and the rate-of-zero law says give it its own arrival source. Do not stage it as timed steps; marketRaise is the pattern, N clamps on one 0..1 progress, so it packs away in reverse for free. And do not trust the 0.9-cell separation to hold by itself: cue c49 says that guarantee is at SPAWN only, and an audience STANDS STILL — which is the case the birds already fail.

queue.brief: Nine systems read season() and every one of them is west of the bridge or in the sky. The plaza is identical in February and August — the exact position the market was in before #29. The fountain is the plaza's landmark and has no seasonal reader at all. Give it the year: what the water does, what the basin looks like, and who is willing to stand near it should not be the same in midwinter as in midsummer.
queue.successLooksLike: A pinned midwinter and a pinned midsummer plaza differ visibly in the wide shot, and the difference is continuous — a probe over a folded year shows no step in the fountain terms at any phase, and every term reduces exactly to today's constant at SEASON_START.
queue.avoid: riverRun() already exists for the water and reads the same year — read it or a sibling of it; do not re-derive a second water-season term (one predicate, one definition). Do not let a global scalar approach zero without per-cell variance or it reads as a switch. And check what the fountain was tuned against before making its constants variable: crumbSpot's keep-rect reads waterBox off the grid, and #24 put 22 birds in the basin the last time two places evaluated the same geometry.

queue.brief: The allotment block is a vegetable block that does not contain only vegetables. The opening scatter seeds ornamentals into the plots — seed 42 opens with a fern in the block, seed 7 with a fern and a lavender — because speciesFor() filters only NEW sowing, not the initial scatter. Since #29 that matters in a way it did not before: harvestPlot() pays its cells into produce[], stockMarket() lays them out, and the town can now put a fern on a market stall as something a gardener grew to sell. Make the block vegetables from the first frame.
queue.successLooksLike: Over ten seeds, no non-vegetable species ever occupies an allotment plot at t=0 or reaches mkShelf at any point in a folded year, and the courtyard beds are unchanged — the same eleven species in the same proportions as HEAD, proven against a stashed baseline.
queue.avoid: Do not fix it by filtering at the market — that is a second predicate for what an allotment grows and it will drift from speciesFor(). Fix it where the block is populated. Expect the census to churn everywhere: any change to the opening scatter reshuffles the seeded world, so read the diff for collapse, not delta.

queue.brief: #27 taught the pointer to name what it is over, and it names ground, plants and trees. Every living thing in the town — the walkers, the cafe sitters, the ducks, the swans, the sweeper, the cat, the person in the boat — passes under that same pointer and answers with the paving it happens to be standing on. Name the people and the animals too, in the town's own register, so a viewer pointing at the obvious moving thing is told what it is rather than what is under its feet.
queue.successLooksLike: Pointing at a walker, a duck, a swan, the sweeper or the boat names that thing and not the paving; a probe finds zero cells where a person is drawn and the ground wins; the name follows a moving figure without flickering as it walks, and clears cleanly when it leaves.
queue.avoid: Do not hit-test in world space — people are drawn as sprites at a screen position, and crowns[] is the pattern #27 established for exactly this (a second derivation of the same geometry is what drifts). Do not read a per-agent countdown field as a stable label: a.timer, a.greet and a.watch all cycle several times a second. One read per FRAME off the last pointer position, as #27 does — not per mousemove.
